questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Electromagnetic waves travel in a medium with a speed of $\text{2} \times {\text{10}^{8} \text{m}s^{- 1}.$ The relative permeability of the medium is $1$. Find the relative permittivity.
questions.solution:
Here, $\text{v} = 2 \times {10}^{8} \text{m}s^{- 1}$ and ${μ}_{r} = 1$

The speed of electromagnetic waves in a medium is given by

$\text{v} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\text{\mu} \text{ε}}} \text{,} \text{....(i)}$

where $\mu$ and $ε$ are absolute permeability and absolute permittivity of the medium.

Now, $\mu = {μ}_{0} {μ}_{r}$ and $ε = {ε}_{0} {ε}_{r}$

Therefore, the equation (i) becomes

$\text{v} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{{μ}_{0} {μ}_{r} \times {ε}_{0} {ε}_{r}}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{{μ}_{0} {ε}_{0}}} \times \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{{μ}_{r} {ε}_{r}}} = \dfrac{\text{c}}{\sqrt{{μ}_{r} {ε}_{r}}}$

$\text{or} {ε}_{r} = \dfrac{c^{2}}{v^{2} {μ}_{r}} = \dfrac{{\left(3 \times {10}^{8}\right)}^{2}}{{\left(2 \times {10}^{8}\right)}^{2} \times 1} = \text{2.25}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The magnetic field of a plane electromagnetic wave is given by $\overset{→}{B} = {B}_{0}\overset{^}{i}  \left[cos \left(kz - \omegat\right)\right] + {B}_{1}\overset{^}{j}cos\left(kz + \omegat\right)$, where ${B}_{0} = 3 \times {10}^{– 5}T$ and ${B}_{1} = 2 \times {10}^{– 6}T$. The RMS value of the force experienced by a stationary charge $Q = {10}^{– 4}C$ at $z = 0 is closest to$
questions.solution:
$\overset{→}{B} = {B}_{0}\overset{^}{i} \left[cos \left(kz - \omegat\right)\right] + {B}_{1}\overset{^}{j}cos\left(kz + \omegat\right)$
${B}_{0} = 3 \times {10}^{- 5}T{B}_{1} = 2 \times {10}^{- 6}T$
Electric filed associated with it is,
$\overset{→}{E} = - {B}_{0}c\overset{^}{j}cos \left(kz - \omegat\right) - {B}_{1}c\overset{^}{i}cos\left(kz + \omegat\right)$
Here, c is speed of light in vacuum.
At $z = 0,$
${F}_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{{\left(Q{B}_{0}c\right)}^{2} + {\left(Q{B}_{1}c\right)}^{2}}{2}}$
Here $c$ is speed of light in vacuum.
$= \sqrt{\dfrac{{ \left({10}^{- 4} \times 3 \times {10}^{- 5} \times 3 \times {10}^{8}\right)}^{2} + { \left({10}^{- 4} \times 2 \times {10}^{- 6} \times 3 \times {10}^{8}\right)}^{2}}{2}}$
$= \sqrt{\dfrac{0.81 + 0.0036}{2}} =$0.6N

questions.q: A& $50Wm^{- 2}$energy density of sunlight is incident normally on the surface of a solar panel. Some part of incident energy ($25 %$) is reflected from the surface and the rest is absorbed. The force exerted on $1m^{2}$ surface area will be close to $\left(c = 3 \times {10}^{8}ms^{- 1}\right)$
questions.solution:
The pressure exerted by the photons

$P = 0.75 \times \dfrac{I}{c} + 0.25 \times \dfrac{2I}{c}$ ( $P$ = pressure, $c$ = speed of light, $I$ = intensity )

$P = 1.25 \times \dfrac{I}{c}$

We know the force can be computed using

$F = P \times A$ & ( $F$ = force, $P$ = pressure, $A$ = area )

$F = 1.25 \times \left(\dfrac{50 \times 1}{3 \times 1{0}^{8}}\right)

$F = 20.83 $\times1{0}^{- 8}N$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The intensity of $\gamma$ - radiation from a given source is $I$. On passing through $36$ mm of lead, it is reduced to $\dfrac{I}{8}$. Assuming that the intensity in transmitted radiation varies exponentially with the thickness of the material, then the thickness of lead, which will reduce the intensity to $\dfrac{I}{2}$, will be&
questions.solution:
On passing through lead, the intensity of $\gamma$ - radiation decreases exponentially with the thickness traversed and is given by$

$I = {I}_{0}e^{- \mux}$ , where $\mu$ is the absorption coefficient of the lead.$

In the first case, when $x = 36mm$, $I = \dfrac{{I}_{0}}{8}$

$\dfrac{I0}{8} = {I}_{0}e^{- \mu \times 36}$

$⇒ \log_{\mathrm{e}}8 = 36\mu$

In the second case,$

$I = $\dfrac{I0}{2}

Let $x$ be the thickness of the lead sheet, then$

$\dfrac{{I}_{0}}{2} = {I}_{0}e^{- \mux}$

$\log_{\mathrm{e}} ⁡ 2 = \mux$

$\dfrac{\mux}{36\mu} = \dfrac{\log_{\mathrm{e}}2}{\log_{\mathrm{e}}8}$

$x = 36 \times \dfrac{\log_{\mathrm{e}} ⁡ 2}{\log_{\mathrm{e}} ⁡ {2}^{3}} = 36 \times \dfrac{\log_{\mathrm{e}} ⁡ 2}{3\log_{\mathrm{e}} ⁡ 2}$

$x = 12mm$

questions.q: An oil drop carrying a charge $q$ has a mass $m$ kg. It is falling freely in air with terminal speed $v$. The electric field required to make the drop move upwards with the same speed is
questions.solution:
$\dfrac{\text{QV}}{ℓ} = \dfrac{4}{3} \pi r^{3} ρ \text{g}$

When the oil drop is falling freely under the effect of gravity is a viscous medium with terminal speed $v,$ then

$mg = 6\piηrv$ ...(i)

To move the oil drop upward with terminal velocity $v$ if $E$ is the electric field intensity applied, the

$Eq = mg + 6\piηrv = mg + mg = 2mg$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A tiny spherical oil drop carrying a net charge $q$ is balanced in still air with vertical uniform electric field of strength $\dfrac{81\pi}{7} \times {10}^{5}Vm^{- 1} .$ When the field is switched off, the drop is observed to fall with terminal velocity$2 \times {10}^{- 3}\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm{ms}^{-1} .$ Given $g = 9.8{ms}^{- 2},$ viscosity of the air =$1.8 \times {10}^{- 5}Nsm^{- 2}$ and the density of oil $= 900kgm^{- 3},$ the magnitude of $q$ is
questions.solution:
$qE = mg$ ...(i)

$6\piηrv = mg$

$\dfrac{4}{3}\pir^{3}ρg = mg$ ...(ii)

$∴ r = {\left(\dfrac{3mg}{4\piρg}\right)}^{1 / 3}$ ...(iii)

Substituting the value of r in Eq. (ii), we get

$6\piηv{\left(\dfrac{3mg}{4\piρg}\right)}^{1 / 3} = mg$

or~${\left(6\piηv\right)}^{3}\left(\dfrac{3mg}{4\piρg}\right) = {\left(mg\right)}^{3}$

Again substituting $mg = qE,$we get

$\left(qE\right)2 = \left(\dfrac{3}{4\piρg}\right)\left(6\piηv\right)3$

Or $qE = {\left(\dfrac{3}{4\piρg}\right)}^{1 / 2}{\left(6\piηv\right)}^{3 / 2}$

$∴ q = \dfrac{1}{E}\left(\dfrac{3}{4\piρg}\right)\dfrac{1}{2}\left(6\piηv\right)3 / 2$

Substituting the values, we get

$q = \dfrac{7}{81\pi \times {10}^{5}}\sqrt{\dfrac{3}{4\pi \times 900 \times 9.8} \times 216{\pi}^{3}}$

$\times \sqrt{\left(1.8 \times {10}^{- 5} \times 2 \times {10}^{- 3}\right)3} = 8.0 \times {10}^{- 19}C$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Cathode rays of velocity ${10}^{6}\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm{ms}^{-1}$ describe an approximately circular path of radius 1 m in an electric field $300{Vm}^{- 1}.$ If the velocity of cathode rays are doubled. The value of electric field so that the rays describe the same circular path, will be
questions.solution:
Cathode rays are composed of electrons, when they move in electric field a force

$F = eE$...(i)

Acts on them, this provides the necessary centripetal force to the particles

$F = \dfrac{mv^{2}}{r}$...(ii)

From Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get

$eE = \dfrac{mv^{2}}{r}$

$⇒ r = \dfrac{mv^{2}}{eE} = \dfrac{m{\left({10}^{6}\right)}^{2}}{e ( 300 )}$...(iii)

When velocity is doubled same circular path is followed, hence radius is same

$r = \dfrac{m{\left(2 \times {10}^{6}\right)}^{2}}{eE}$...(iv)

Equating Eqs. (iii) and (iv), we get

$m \times \dfrac{{\left({10}^{6}\right)}^{2}}{300e} = \dfrac{m \times {\left(2 \times {10}^{6}\right)}^{2}}{eE}$

$⇒ E = 300 \times 4 = 1200$ V $ cm^{- 1}$
